issues.legal_issue: A father governed by Mitakshara law cannot make a testamentary disposition of ancestral property in which his sons have acquired an interest by birth.
material_facts: The father described the properties in the relevant schedules as family or tarvad properties.
The instrument purported to deal with the whole of those properties, including the sons’ interests, rather than only the father’s own undivided share.
The father retained powers of disposition during his lifetime and intended the directions concerning the properties to take effect after his death.
issues.conclusion: The instrument was ineffective as a will insofar as it purported to dispose of ancestral property.
issues.legal_principle: A Mitakshara father has no authority to make a will disposing of ancestral property in which his sons have acquired an interest by birth. The Court relied on the characterization of the property as joint family property and distinguished a testamentary disposition of the father’s own undivided share, which was not attempted here.

predicates.validity_of_will_in_joint_family_propert: The proceeding concerns whether an instrument is effective as a will in a dispute over joint family property.
predicates.ancestral_joint_property: The property was ancestral joint family property in which the sons had acquired interests by birth.
predicates.father_attempted_to_dispose_of_sons_inte: The father purported by will to dispose of the sons’ interests in the ancestral property, rather than only his own undivided share.

issues.definition: When a will in a joint family property dispute purports to dispose of ancestral property interests acquired by sons by birth, the testamentary disposition is ineffective.

issues.legal_issue: A Mitakshara father joint with his sons may unilaterally disrupt their joint family status as part of exercising his power to partition the family property.
material_facts: The father was joint with his sons and governed by Mitakshara law.
The instrument specified the shares intended for each son and made provision to correct an imbalance in the allocations.
The father’s instrument did not divide the property by metes and bounds in the present, and reserved his power to deal with the property during his lifetime.
issues.conclusion: The father’s power to partition included the power to bring about a disruption of joint family status, even though the instrument did not effect a present division of property by metes and bounds.
issues.legal_principle: A Mitakshara father joint with his sons has a broader power than an ordinary coparcener or manager: he may partition family property between himself and his sons and among the sons without their consent. That power includes the initial step of disrupting joint family status. The Court relied on Mitakshara law as discussed in Mayne’s Hindu Law and Usage and Mulla’s Hindu Law, and on Kandaswami v. Doraiswami Ayyar.

predicates.mitakshara_father_sons_partition_dispute: The proceeding concerns a proposed partition of family property by a father joint with his sons under Mitakshara law.
predicates.father_joint_with_sons: The father was a member of the joint family with his sons.
predicates.father_specified_family_shares: The father specified shares for family members as part of arranging division of the family property.

issues.definition: In a Mitakshara partition dispute, a joint father who specifies family shares can unilaterally disrupt the joint family status as part of his partition power.

issues.legal_issue: An ineffective will does not bind family members as a family arrangement without the required agreement and assent, and a father cannot impose such an arrangement merely by exercising his partition power.
material_facts: The instrument was ineffective as a will and was not intended to operate from the date of execution.
There was no evidence that the adult family members entitled to shares had agreed to its terms when it was executed.
There was no evidence of a family dispute being compromised or of an arrangement needed to preserve family property or family security.
The evidence that male members acted according to the father’s wishes after his death did not establish their agreement to a family arrangement when the instrument was made.
issues.conclusion: The instrument did not establish a binding family arrangement.
issues.legal_principle: A family arrangement must be intended generally and reasonably for the family’s benefit and must aim to compromise doubtful or disputed rights or preserve family property or family security. It must be assented to by those affected; an ineffective will may operate as a family arrangement if consent and the other requirements are established. The Court relied on M.N. Aryamurthy v. M.D. Subbaraya Setty, Brijraj Singh v. Sheodan Singh, and Lakshmi Chand v. Anandi.

rule.if: family_arrangement_claim_in_joint_family_dispute and ineffective_will_relied_on_as_arrangement and (not evidence_of_assent_when_made or not evidence_of_family_purpose)

predicates.family_arrangement_claim_in_joint_family: The proceeding concerns a claim that an instrument binds family members as a family arrangement.
predicates.ineffective_will_relied_on_as_arrangemen: A party relies on an instrument that is ineffective as a will as the asserted family arrangement.
predicates.evidence_of_assent_when_made: The family members whose rights are affected agreed to the arrangement when it was made.
predicates.evidence_of_family_purpose: The arrangement was made to benefit the family by settling doubtful or disputed rights or preserving family property or family security.

issues.definition: An ineffective will relied on as a family arrangement does not bind affected family members if assent when it was made or a qualifying family purpose is not established.

issues.legal_issue: When a father’s instrument specifies and allocates individual shares, the coparcenary is disrupted, and the remaining members do not continue as coparceners merely because they are grouped by their mothers or continue to live and work together.
material_facts: The instrument specified the share of each son and allocated properties to the sons, while also providing for other family members and an adjustment for unequal allocations.
The instrument used terms describing family branches associated with the two wives.
After the son from the second marriage took his allotted share and left, the other sons remained under one roof, shared food, and worked together.
There was no evidence of an agreement by the remaining sons to continue jointly or of a reunion in the legal sense.
issues.conclusion: The family status was disrupted and the remaining sons held their property as tenants-in-common, not as coparceners with survivorship rights; the wife-based grouping did not create a separate coparcenary.
issues.legal_principle: A definite and unequivocal indication of an intention to separate, known to those affected, can sever joint family status; severance entails division of rights even if there is no immediate physical division by metes and bounds. Once shares are defined, subsequent conduct or shared enjoyment does not alter the legal effect absent reunion. There is no presumption that the remaining members stay joint when one member separates, and coparcenary cannot be created by agreement except in the case of reunion. Mitakshara law does not recognize wife-wise branches as separate coparcenary units. The Court relied on Appovier v. Rama Subha Aiyar, Raghavamma v. Chenchamma, Palani Ammal v. Muthuvenkatachala Moniagar, Bhagwan Dayal v. Smt. Reoti Devi, Balabux v. Rukhmabai, Bhagwati Prasad Shah v. Dulhin Rameshwari Juer, Balkishen Das v. Ram Narain Sahu, and Boddu Venkatakrishna Rao v. Boddu Satyavathi.

rule.if: mitakshara_joint_family_partition_dispute and unequivocal_individual_shares_allocated and (member_took_share_and_separated or family_status_was_otherwise_severed) and not reunion_proved and wife_based_branches_claimed

predicates.mitakshara_joint_family_partition_disput: The proceeding concerns the status and property interests of members of a Mitakshara joint family.
predicates.unequivocal_individual_shares_allocated: A person with power to partition specified and allocated individual shares in the family property.
predicates.member_took_share_and_separated: A family member took the allotted share and left the family.
predicates.family_status_was_otherwise_severed: The family’s joint status was otherwise severed by a definite and unequivocal indication of separation known to those affected.
predicates.reunion_proved: The remaining members agreed to reunite or otherwise established a reunion in the legal sense.
predicates.wife_based_branches_claimed: A party claimed that members grouped according to their mothers formed separate coparcenary branches.

issues.definition: Where individual shares are unequivocally allocated and the family status is severed, the remaining members hold as tenants-in-common without survivorship unless reunion is proved; grouping members by their mothers does not create a coparcenary.

issues.legal_issue: A widow may claim her deceased husband’s share in property held by the family as tenants-in-common, but she cannot claim a share in separately owned properties on the record where concurrent findings establish that they were not family-property accretions.
material_facts: The deceased husband was one of four sons who held the relevant scheduled property as tenants-in-common after the joint family status was disrupted.
The plaintiff sought a share in that property as her deceased husband’s widow.
The trial court and High Court found that the other two schedules comprised property belonging to a defendant and his wife and were not accretions to the property that had devolved from the father.
The Supreme Court found those concurrent findings supported by the evidence.
issues.conclusion: The plaintiff was entitled to a one-quarter share in the first schedule, and a preliminary decree was ordered for that share; her claims to the second and third schedules remained dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: After severance of joint family status, the members hold as tenants-in-common and a deceased member’s share does not pass by survivorship. The Court applied that conclusion to the deceased husband’s share and left undisturbed the concurrent factual findings that the other properties were separately owned and not accretions to the family property.

predicates.partition_suit: The proceeding is a suit seeking partition and separate possession of property.
predicates.family_property_held_as_tenants_in_commo: The relevant family property was held by the family members as tenants-in-common rather than as a coparcenary with survivorship.
predicates.deceased_member_had_defined_share: The claimant’s deceased predecessor held a defined share in the property.
predicates.claimant_succeeds_to_deceased_members_sh: The claimant is entitled to succeed to the deceased predecessor’s share.

issues.definition: In a partition suit, a claimant who succeeds to a deceased member’s defined share is entitled to that share when the property is held as tenants-in-common.
